Global smooth solutions for triangular reaction-cross diffusion systems

Jessica Guerand Jessica GuerandIMAG, Université de Montpellier, 499-554 Rue du Truel, 34090 Montpellier, France Email address: jessica.guerand@umontpellier.fr , Angeliki Menegaki Angeliki MenegakiInstitut des hautes études Scientifiques, 35 Rte de Chartres, 91440, Bures-sur-Yvette, France Email address: menegaki@ihes.fr and Ariane Trescases Ariane TrescasesIMT; UMR5219, Université de Toulouse; CNRS, F-31400 Toulouse, France Email address: ariane.trescases@math.univ-toulouse.fr
Abstract.

For a class of reaction cross-diffusion systems of two equations with a cross-diffusion term in the first equation and with self-diffusion terms, we prove that the unique local smooth solution given by Amann theorem is actually global. This class of systems arises in Population dynamics, and extends the triangular Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto system when general power-laws growth are considered in the reaction and diffusion rates.

1. Introduction

1.1. The system

The purpose of this article is to study the global existence of a smooth solution of the following system,

∂tu−Δ⁡((du+dα​⟨u⟩α+dβ​⟨v⟩β)​u)=u⁡(ru−ra​⟨u⟩a−rb​⟨v⟩b),in[0,∞)×Ω,∂tv−Δ⁡((dv+dγ​⟨v⟩γ)​v)=v⁡(rv−rc​⟨v⟩c−rd​⟨u⟩d),in[0,∞)×Ω,∇u⋅n=∇v⋅n=0,in[0,∞)×∂Ω,u(0,⋅)=u0,v(0,⋅)=v0,in​Ω,\begin{array}[]{rl}\partial_{t}u-\Delta\Big((d_{u}+d_{\alpha}\langle u\rangle^{\alpha}+d_{\beta}\langle v\rangle^{\beta})u\Big)=u(r_{u}-r_{a}\langle u\rangle^{a}-r_{b}\langle v\rangle^{b}),&\text{in}\ [0,\infty)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta\big((d_{v}+d_{\gamma}\langle v\rangle^{\gamma})v\big)=v(r_{v}-r_{c}\langle v\rangle^{c}-r_{d}\langle u\rangle^{d}),&\text{in}\ [0,\infty)\times\Omega,\\ \nabla u\cdot n=\nabla v\cdot n=0,&\text{in}\ [0,\infty)\times\partial\Omega,\\ u(0,\cdot)=u_{0},\quad v(0,\cdot)=v_{0},&\text{in}\ \Omega,\end{array} (1.1)

with the bracket ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle defined by

⟨z⟩:=(1+z2)1/2,z≥0,\langle z\rangle:=\left(1+z^{2}\right)^{1/2},\qquad z\geq 0, (1.2)

and where u=u⁡(t,x)≥0u=u(t,x)\geq 0 and v=v⁡(t,x)≥0v=v(t,x)\geq 0 are the unknowns, Ω\Omega is a smooth open bounded domain of ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m} for m≥2m\geq 2 and n⁡(x)n(x) is the outward normal vector at point x∈∂Ωx\in\partial\Omega. The functions u0,v0:Ω→ℝu_{0},v_{0}:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R} are nonnegative initial data belonging to C2+νC^{2+\nu} for some ν>0\nu>0. The constant parameters are defined in the set DD,

D:={du,dv,dα,dβ,dγ,ru,rv,ra,rb,rc,rd,a,b,c,d,α,β,γ}∈((0,∞))17×[0,∞),D:=\{d_{u},d_{v},d_{\alpha},d_{\beta},d_{\gamma},r_{u},r_{v},r_{a},r_{b},r_{c},r_{d},a,b,c,d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}\in\left((0,\infty)\right)^{17}\times[0,\infty), (1.3)

and are assumed to satisfy

d<12​max⁡{1+a,2+α,a+α,2​α+2/m}andd<max⁡(8​α​(m+1)(m2−4)+,4​α+2​am+2),d<\frac{1}{2}\max\{1+a,2+\alpha,a+\alpha,2\alpha+2/m\}\quad\text{and}\quad d<\max\left(\frac{8\alpha(m+1)}{(m^{2}-4)_{+}},\frac{4\alpha+2a}{m+2}\right), (1.4)

where we recall that mm is the space dimension. This system is a prototypical extension of the triangular Shigasada-Kawasaki-Teramoto system arising in Population dynamics, [SKT79]:

∂tu−Δ⁡((du+dα​u+dβ​v)​u)=u⁡(ru−ra​u−rb​v),in[0,∞)×Ω,∂tv−Δ⁡((dv+dγ​v)​v)=v⁡(rv−rc​v−rd​u),in[0,∞)×Ω,\begin{array}[]{rl}\partial_{t}u-\Delta\Big((d_{u}+d_{\alpha}u+d_{\beta}v)u\Big)=u(r_{u}-r_{a}u-r_{b}v),&\text{in}\ [0,\infty)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta\big((d_{v}+d_{\gamma}v)v\big)=v(r_{v}-r_{c}v-r_{d}u),&\text{in}\ [0,\infty)\times\Omega,\end{array} (1.5)

when the linear terms in the reaction and diffusion rates are replaced with functionals with a power law growth at infinity. System (1.5) and its extension System (1.1) model the evolution of the space densities of the populations of two living species interacting through their movement. The terms dα​⟨u⟩α​ud_{\alpha}\langle u\rangle^{\alpha}u and dγ​⟨v⟩γ​vd_{\gamma}\langle v\rangle^{\gamma}v are the self-diffusion terms, and dβ​⟨v⟩β​ud_{\beta}\langle v\rangle^{\beta}u is the cross-diffusion term. In the diffusion rates, we use the bracket ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle taken at some powers α\alpha, β\beta or γ\gamma to guarantee a smooth behaviour close to zero even for powers α\alpha, β\beta or γ\gamma less than one. When the power α\alpha, β\beta or γ\gamma respectively is greater or equal to one, one could replace the term ⟨u⟩α\langle u\rangle^{\alpha}, ⟨v⟩β\langle v\rangle^{\beta} or ⟨v⟩γ\langle v\rangle^{\gamma} respectively, by the simpler power law term uαu^{\alpha}, vβv^{\beta} or vγv^{\gamma} respectively, and our results would still apply. The same applies for the reaction rates ⟨u⟩a\langle u\rangle^{a}, ⟨v⟩b\langle v\rangle^{b}, ⟨v⟩c\langle v\rangle^{c} and ⟨u⟩d\langle u\rangle^{d}.

By considering System (1.1) instead of the original system (1.5) we follow the idea of replacing linear interaction rates by more general nonlinear terms. This idea goes back to the studies of [GJ72, GA73] where some non-linear functions were proved to be more appropriate than linear ones to model the competitive interaction between two species (in their study, two species of drosophila), modelled in that case with an ordinary differential system. We use power laws for simplicity, though a wide range of functions could be considered. Such generalized (triangular) Shigasada-Kawasaki-Teramoto systems have been studied for example in [PT90, Wan05, Yam95, DT15, Tre16].

1.2. Main result

Our main result is the following.

Theorem 1 (Global smooth solutions).

Let Ω\Omega be a bounded open subset of ℝm{\mathbb{R}}^{m} such that ∂Ω\partial\Omega is smooth. Let the coefficients of (1.1) satisfy (1.3)–(1.4) and u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} be nonnegative functions in C2+ν​(Ω¯)C^{2+\nu}(\overline{\Omega}) for some ν>0\nu>0 satisfying the Neumann boundary condition

∇u0⋅n=∇v0⋅n=0 on ∂Ω.\nabla u_{0}\cdot n=\nabla v_{0}\cdot n=0\quad\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega.

Then the system possesses a unique, nonnegative, global solution (u,v)(u,v) such that

u,v∈C2+ν2,2+ν​([0,∞)×Ω¯)∩C∞​((0,∞)×Ω¯).u,v\in C^{\frac{2+\nu}{2},2+\nu}([0,\infty)\times\overline{\Omega})\cap C^{\infty}((0,\infty)\times\overline{\Omega}).

To prove this theorem, we rely on Amann’s results which gives the local existence of a unique smooth solution together with an extension criteria (for a large classs of system including (1.1), see [Ama90, Ama89, Ama93]). More precisely, for System (1.1), Amann’s result reads as follows.

Theorem 2 (Local smooth solutions [Ama90, Ama89, Ama93]).

Let Ω\Omega be a bounded open subset of ℝm{\mathbb{R}}^{m} such that ∂Ω\partial\Omega is smooth. Let the coefficients of (1.1) satisfy (1.3) and u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} be nonnegative functions in W1,p0​(Ω)W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega) with p0>mp_{0}>m. Then there exists a maximal time tmax∈(0,∞]t_{\mathrm{max}}\in\left(0,\infty\right] such that the system (1.1) has a unique nonnegative solution (u,v)(u,v) in (0,tmax)×Ω\left(0,t_{\mathrm{max}}\right)\times\Omega such that

u,v∈C⁡([0,tmax),W1,p0​(Ω))∩C∞​((0,tmax)×Ω¯),u,v\in C([0,t_{\mathrm{max}}),W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega))\cap C^{\infty}((0,t_{\mathrm{max}})\times\overline{\Omega}),

Moreover, if tmax<∞t_{\mathrm{max}}<\infty, then

limt→tmax−[‖u⁡(t,⋅)‖W1,p0​(Ω)+‖v⁡(t,⋅)‖W1,p0​(Ω)]=∞.\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow t^{-}_{\mathrm{max}}}\left[\left\|u(t,\cdot)\right\|_{W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega)}+\left\|v(t,\cdot)\right\|_{W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega)}\right]=\infty.

1.3. State of the art

The local existence of smooth solutions together with an extension criteria for a wide class of parabolic systems including (1.1) was established by Amann in [Ama90, Ama89, Ama93], as stated in Theorem 2.

For global existence, many works focus on the original (quadratic) triangular Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto system (1.5). When there is self-diffusion in the first equation, that is when dα>0d_{\alpha}>0, the existence of global smooth solutions was first established in dimensions m=1m=1 and m=2m=2, [LNW98, Yag93], then in dimension m≤5m\leq 5 in [CLY04, LNN03], then m≤9m\leq 9 in [VT08]. Finally, Hoang et al. recently extended these results to any dimension m≥1m\geq 1 in [HNP15]. Their method rely on De Giorgi techniques and on the proof of a Sobolev regularity result for nonlinear parabolic scalar equations with self-diffusion. We also mention the interesting work of [TW19] where the authors show that for the case dα>0d_{\alpha}>0, in convex domains of dimension m≤9m\leq 9, the global solutions are uniformly bounded and the long-time behaviour is studied. The situation without self-diffusion in the first equation (dα=0d_{\alpha}=0) is more delicate, and global smooth solutions have been obtained only in dimension m=2m=2 in [LNW98], with the exception of the case with no self diffusion at all (dα=dγ=0d_{\alpha}=d_{\gamma}=0) which is treated in any dimension m≥1m\geq 1 in [CLY04] and [DT15]. However, global weak solutions exist in any dimension mm even for the case dα=0d_{\alpha}=0 and dγ>0d_{\gamma}>0: see [Tre16].

Let us now present works on more generic forms of triangular cross-diffusion systems allowing for power law growth in the spirit of (1.1). In absence of self-diffusion terms, that is α=γ=0\alpha=\gamma=0, global smooth solutions were obtained in [PT90] with assumptions on the reaction part that amount to assume a fast decay in uu of the reaction terms and in [Yam95] when a>da>d. Global weak solutions were furthermore obtained in [DT15] in the same case a>da>d and when a≤1a\leq 1 and d≤2d\leq 2 (without the brackets ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle). Allowing the presence of self-diffusion, global existence has been obtained in [Wan05] in the case α>0\alpha>0, γ=0\gamma=0 under a (dimension-dependent) condition of smallness of the parameter dd w.r.t. the parameter aa. Then, global weak solutions were obtained in [Tre16] when the powers satisfy: (α>0,d<2+α,a<1+α)(\alpha>0,d<2+\alpha,a<1+\alpha) or (α=0,d≤2,a≤1)(\alpha=0,d\leq 2,a\leq 1), with no condition on γ\gamma other that nonnegativity (and again, without the need of the brackets ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle). We also mention here the recent paper [Le21] where regularity criteria leading to uniqueness of a specific weak-strong notion of solutions are provided for a class of cross-diffusion systems.

In the general case where γ\gamma can be positive, smooth solutions were not studied, which is the purpose of the present work. The case γ>0\gamma>0 is the most delicate case, as one can not rely on the properties of the heat operator: see Remark 4. In particular, for the original SKT system (1.5), we observe from the literature that the presence of self-diffusion in the first equation α>0\alpha>0 is crucial to obtain regularity. Here, we want to investigate how much self-diffusion, quantified by the parameter α\alpha, is actually enough to obtain smooth solutions for the more general system (1.1). A first answer is given by the assumption (1.4). However, we give in the following subsection some possible relaxations of these assumptions.

1.4. Strategy of the proof and possible extensions

Our strategy of proof relies on the following main ingredients: first we apply Amann’s theorem to obtain local smooth solutions on [0,tmax)[0,t_{\mathrm{max}}), and the objective is to extend them globally. Let T∈(0,∞)T\in(0,\infty) with T≤tmaxT\leq t_{\mathrm{max}}. Our objective is to prove that the local solution satisfy

supt∈(0,T)‖u⁡(t,⋅)‖W1,p0​(Ω)+‖v⁡(t,⋅)‖W1,p0​(Ω)<∞,\sup_{t\in(0,T)}\left\|u(t,\cdot)\right\|_{W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega)}+\left\|v(t,\cdot)\right\|_{W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega)}<\infty, (1.6)

so that necessarily by Theorem 2, the unique local solution in Theorem 2 is global, which gives Theorem 1.

Our first basic estimates are the maximum principle for vv and a combination of a duality estimate and an energy-type estimate coming from the logistic-type growth for uu. Then, we iterate some higher-order energy-type estimates for uu and classical parabolic regularity estimates for vv in Sobolev spaces in order to obtain that both uu and ∇v\nabla v are in Lp​((0,T)×Ω)L^{p}((0,T)\times\Omega) for all p>1p>1. We then obtain that uu is bounded by defining a class of energy estimate that allows us to use De Giorgi method. And finally we conclude using the classical Hölder and Schauder estimates.

We list in the following remarks some possible extensions of this result and perspectives.

Remark 3 (The case α=0\alpha=0).

When α>0\alpha>0, the self-diffusion in the first equation allows to prove more regularity for uu. This appears in our assumption (1.4), and can also be seen directly for example in the duality estimate which gives a bound for uu in L2+αL^{2+\alpha}. The case where α=0\alpha=0 is an unfavorable case. It is actually covered by our method when the reaction parameters aa and dd satisfy d⁡(m+2)<2​ad(m+2)<2a.

Remark 4 (The case γ=0\gamma=0).

The case where there is no self-diffusion in the second equation, that is γ=0\gamma=0, is a very favorable case. In this case, the properties of the heat operator allow to obtain regularity for the first and second space derivatives of vv without any dimension-dependent assumption, and this even in the unfavorable case where there is no self-diffusion in the first equation. For example, the results hold under the condition γ=0\gamma=0, α=0\alpha=0, d<ad<a, see [Yam95] or [DT15].

Remark 5 (Dimension-dependent assumptions).

We expect that our result holds for larger range for dd rather than d<max⁡(8​α​(m+1)(m2−4)+,4​α+2​am+2)d<\max\left(\frac{8\alpha(m+1)}{(m^{2}-4)_{+}},\frac{4\alpha+2a}{m+2}\right). We use this assumption in the proof of Lemma 16 in order to obtain the continuity of vv (thanks to dimension-dependent embeddings), which allows to apply classical results of parabolic regularity in Sobolev spaces: see the result due to Ladyzenskaya et al. stated later in Lemma 14. In fact, for the original system (1.5) we recover the results in [VT08] with the same restriction on the dimension, see also [TW19]. However, some recent results for the original system (1.5) due to Hoang et al., [HNP15], suggest that we can bypass this classical tool and obtain directly estimates on the gradient of vv in any LpL^{p} space, conditionally to the LpL^{p} regularity of the right hand side, without requiring the continuity of vv. The result of Hoang et al. could be extended to system (1.1) with a generic γ>0\gamma>0, and as a consequence we could remove the space-dependent assumption. This is the purpose of an ongoing work.

Remark 6 (Weak solutions).

Using the same techniques we could also prove that the weak solutions obtained in [Tre16] with initial conditions in W2,∞W^{2,\infty}, are actually smooth. In that case one can deduce that the two solutions in [Ama93] and in [Tre16] must coincide.

2. Gain of integrability of ∇xv\nabla_{x}v and uu

In this section we prove that uu and ∇xv\nabla_{x}v are in any LpL^{p} space with p∈(0,∞)p\in(0,\infty). To get this result, we use an iteration process to transfer of regularity between uu and ∇v\nabla v. We first give some basic estimates to initialize the iteration process. Then we give some conditional properties of transfer of regularity between uu and ∇xv\nabla_{x}v and we conclude by iteration.

2.1. Basic estimates

We start with the following basic estimates.

Lemma 7 (Basic estimates).

The solution (u,v)(u,v) of (1.1) satisfies the following bounds

supt∈(0,T)∫Ωu⁡(t,x)​𝑑x≤C,∬ΩTu1+a​(t,x)​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C1​(T),\displaystyle\sup_{t\in(0,T)}\int_{\Omega}u(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x\leq C,\qquad\iint_{\Omega_{T}}u^{1+a}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t\leq C_{1}(T), (2.1)
supt∈(0,T)‖v⁡(t,⋅)‖L∞​(Ω)≤C,\displaystyle\sup_{t\in(0,T)}\|v(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq C, (2.2)

where CC depends only on the initial data, the domain Ω\Omega and the parameters DD, while C1​(T)C_{1}(T) depends linearly on time.

Proof.

Let us integrate the first equation of (1.1) on Ωt\Omega_{t} for t∈(0,T]t\in\left(0,T\right]

∫Ωu⁡(t,x)​𝑑x=∫Ωu⁡(0,x)​𝑑x+∬ΩTu⁡(du−da​⟨u⟩a−db​⟨v⟩b)​𝑑x​𝑑s.\int_{\Omega}u(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x=\int_{\Omega}u(0,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}u\,(d_{u}-d_{a}\langle u\rangle^{a}-d_{b}\langle v\rangle^{b}){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}s. (2.3)

Using the nonnegativity of uu and vv and the fact that du​z−da​z​⟨z⟩a+da2​za+1≤Cd_{u}z-d_{a}z\langle z\rangle^{a}+\frac{d_{a}}{2}z^{a+1}\leq C for all z≥0z\geq 0, we get the estimate using twice (2.3), once for time tt and once for time TT,

∫Ωu⁡(t,x)​𝑑x+∬ΩTda2​u1+a​𝑑x​𝑑t≤∫Ωu⁡(0,x)​𝑑x+C​|Ω|​T,\int_{\Omega}u(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}\frac{d_{a}}{2}u^{1+a}{\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t\leq\int_{\Omega}u(0,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x+C|\Omega|T, (2.4)

which concludes the two first estimates. The last estimate is a direct consequence of the maximum principle. ∎

Lemma 8 (Interpolation Inequality).

Let ww be the function w=(dv+dγ​⟨v⟩γ)​vw=(d_{v}+d_{\gamma}\langle v\rangle^{\gamma})v and p≥1p\geq 1. It holds that

‖w‖L2​p​((0,T),W1,2​p​(Ω))2​p≤C​‖w‖Lp​((0,T),W2,p​(Ω))p.\|w\|_{L^{2p}((0,T),W^{1,2p}(\Omega))}^{2p}\leq C\|w\|^{p}_{L^{p}((0,T),W^{2,p}(\Omega))}.
Proof.

To prove this we use W2,p​(Ω)∩L∞​(Ω)⊂W1,2​p​(Ω)W^{2,p}(\Omega)\cap L^{\infty}(\Omega)\subset W^{1,2p}(\Omega) of [BL12, Theorem 6.4.5 p.153] or [BM19, Theorem 1] which gives

‖w‖W1,2​p​(Ω)≤C​‖w‖L∞​(Ω)θ​‖w‖W2,p​(Ω)1−θ,\|w\|_{W^{1,2p}(\Omega)}\leq C\|w\|^{\theta}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\|w\|^{1-\theta}_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)},

so using θ=12\theta=\frac{1}{2} we have

∫0T‖w‖W1,2​p​(Ω)2​p​𝑑t\displaystyle\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\|w\|_{W^{1,2p}(\Omega)}^{2p}\mathrm{d}t ≤C​∫0T‖w‖L∞​(Ω)2​p​θ​‖w‖W2,p​(Ω)2​p​(1−θ)​𝑑t\displaystyle\leq C\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\|w\|^{2p\theta}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\|w\|^{2p(1-\theta)}_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}\mathrm{d}t
≤C​‖w‖L∞​(ΩT)p​∫0T‖w‖W2,p​(Ω)p​𝑑t\displaystyle\leq C\|w\|^{p}_{L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\|w\|^{p}_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}\mathrm{d}t
≤C​‖w‖Lp​((0,T),W2,p​(Ω))p,\displaystyle\leq C\|w\|^{p}_{L^{p}((0,T),W^{2,p}(\Omega))},

where we have used Lemma 7 to bound the L∞L^{\infty}-norm in the right-hand side.∎

The next basic estimate is a consequence of the following lemma from [DLMT15], Lemma 2.11, which is obtained by duality techniques.

Lemma 9 (Duality estimate).

Let M:[0,T]×Ω→ℝ+M:[0,T]\times\Omega\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{+} be a positive continuous function lower bounded by a positive constant and let ru>0r_{u}>0. Any smooth nonnegative solution of the differential inequality

∂tu−Δ⁡(M​u)≤ru​u​ on ​Ω,\displaystyle\partial_{t}u-\Delta(Mu)\leq r_{u}u\text{ on }\Omega,
∂n(M​u)=0, on ​∂Ω,\displaystyle\partial_{n}(Mu)=0,\text{ on }\partial\Omega,

satisfies the following bound

∬ΩTM​u2≤exp⁡(2​ru​T)×(CΩ2​‖u⁡(0,⋅)‖Hm−1​(Ω)2+u⁡(0,⋅)¯2​∬ΩTM),\displaystyle\iint_{\Omega_{T}}Mu^{2}\leq\exp(2r_{u}T)\times\left(C_{\Omega}^{2}\,\|u(0,\cdot)\|_{H^{-1}_{m}(\Omega)}^{2}+\overline{u(0,\cdot)}^{2}\iint_{\Omega_{T}}M\right),

As a consequence, we get the following duality estimate.

Let (u,v)(u,v) be the solution of (1.1). Then uu satisfies the following bound,

∬ΩTu2+α​(t,x)​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C,\iint_{\Omega_{T}}u^{2+\alpha}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t\leq C, (2.5)

We finally have the following bound on the gradient of vv thanks to our assumptions on the parameters.

Proposition 12 (Integrability of ∇v\nabla v).

‖∇v‖L4​(ΩT)≤C\|\nabla v\|_{L^{4}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C

≤∫Ωv22​(0,x)​𝑑x+∬ΩTv⁡(rv−rc​⟨v⟩c−rd​⟨u⟩d)​𝑑x​𝑑s\displaystyle\leq\int_{\Omega}\frac{v^{2}}{2}(0,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}v\,(r_{v}-r_{c}\langle v\rangle^{c}-r_{d}\langle u\rangle^{d}){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}s

≲\displaystyle\lesssim ∫Ωuρ​(0,x)​𝑑x+∬ΩTuρ−α​|∇v|2​(t,x)​𝑑x​𝑑t+∬ΩTuρ​𝑑x​𝑑t.\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}u^{\rho}(0,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}u^{\rho-\alpha}|\nabla v|^{2}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}u^{\rho}{\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t.

(2.13)

Gathering therefore the relations (2.12), (2.13) and (2.18) together and neglecting the (time-independent) constants, one has the following inequality

∫Ωuρ​(T,x)​𝑑x+1η​∫Ω|∇w|22​(T,x)​𝑑x+∬ΩT|∇uρ2+α2|2(t,x)dxdt+∬ΩTua+ρ(t,x)dxdt+1η∬ΩT(du+dγ⟨v⟩γ+γ​dγ​v2⟨v⟩2−γ)|Δw|2dxdt≲η​∬ΩTu2​ρ−2​α​(t,x)​𝑑x​𝑑t+1η​∬ΩT(1+u2​d)​𝑑x​𝑑t+∬ΩTuρdxdt+∫Ωuρ(0,x)dx+1η∫Ω|∇w|22(0,x)dx.\begin{split}\int_{\Omega}u^{\rho}(T,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x+\frac{1}{\eta}\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla w|^{2}}{2}(T,x)\mathrm{d}x&+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}|\nabla u^{\frac{\rho}{2}+\frac{\alpha}{2}}|^{2}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}u^{a+\rho}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t\\ &+\frac{1}{\eta}\iint_{\Omega_{T}}\left(d_{u}+d_{\gamma}\langle v\rangle^{\gamma}+\frac{\gamma d_{\gamma}v^{2}}{\langle v\rangle^{2-\gamma}}\right)|\Delta w|^{2}\mathrm{d}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t\\ &\lesssim\eta\iint_{\Omega_{T}}u^{2\rho-2\alpha}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t+\frac{1}{\eta}\iint_{\Omega_{T}}\left(1+u^{2d}\right)\mathrm{d}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t\\ &+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}u^{\rho}\mathrm{d}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t+\int_{\Omega}u^{\rho}(0,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x+\frac{1}{\eta}\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla w|^{2}}{2}(0,x)\mathrm{d}x.\end{split} (2.19)

We continue by considering three different cases regarding the values of a,α,ma,\alpha,m and defining an appropriate ρ>1\rho>1 in each case that satisfies ρ>2​α\rho>2\alpha and d<ρ−αd<\rho-\alpha as well. We then estimate the above right-hand side by

η∬ΩTu2​ρ−2​α(t,x)dxdt+1η∬ΩT(1+u2​d)​dx​dt+∬ΩTuρ​(t,x)​dx​dt++∫Ωuρ(0,x)dx+1η∫Ω|∇w|22(0,x)dx≲(η​∬ΩTu2​ρ−2​α​(t,x)​dx​dt+Cη)\begin{split}\eta\iint_{\Omega_{T}}u^{2\rho-2\alpha}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t+\frac{1}{\eta}\iint_{\Omega_{T}}&\left(1+u^{2d}\right)\mathrm{d}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t+\iint_{\Omega_{T}}u^{\rho}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t+\\ &+\int_{\Omega}u^{\rho}(0,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x+\frac{1}{\eta}\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla w|^{2}}{2}(0,x)\mathrm{d}x\\  &\lesssim\left(\eta\iint_{\Omega_{T}}u^{2\rho-2\alpha}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t+C_{\eta}\right)\end{split} (2.20)

for some positive constant CηC_{\eta}.

Case 1: max⁡(1+a,2+α,a+α,4​α+4/m)=max⁡(1+a,2+α)\max(1+a,2+\alpha,a+\alpha,4\alpha+4/m)=\max(1+a,2+\alpha).

Let ρ:=α+max⁡(1+a,2+α)/2>1\rho:=\alpha+\max(1+a,2+\alpha)/2>1, so that 2​ρ−2​α≤max⁡(1+a,2+α)2\rho-2\alpha\leq\max(1+a,2+\alpha). Then by equation (2.5), we have that u2​ρ−2​αu^{2\rho-2\alpha} is in L1​(ΩT)L^{1}(\Omega_{T}). Therefore, after an integration in time, taking η=1\eta=1 and using the initial regularity,

∫Ωuρ​(T,x)​𝑑x+∫Ω|∇w|22​(T,x)​𝑑x+∫0T∫Ω|∇uρ2+α2|2(t,x)dxdt+∫0T∫Ωua+ρ(t,x)dxdt+∫0T∫Ω(du+dγ⟨v⟩γ+γ​dγ​v2⟨v⟩2−γ)|Δw|2dxdt≤C(T).\begin{split}\int_{\Omega}u^{\rho}(T,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x+\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla w|^{2}}{2}(T,x)\mathrm{d}x&+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u^{\frac{\rho}{2}+\frac{\alpha}{2}}|^{2}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}u^{a+\rho}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t\\ &+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\left(d_{u}+d_{\gamma}\langle v\rangle^{\gamma}+\frac{\gamma d_{\gamma}v^{2}}{\langle v\rangle^{2-\gamma}}\right)|\Delta w|^{2}\mathrm{d}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t\leq C(T).\end{split} (2.21)

Case 2: max⁡(1+a,2+α,a+α,4​α+4/m)=a+α\max(1+a,2+\alpha,a+\alpha,4\alpha+4/m)=a+\alpha. Let ρ:=2​α+a>1\rho:=2\alpha+a>1, and therefore, 2​ρ−2​α=ρ+a2\rho-2\alpha=\rho+a, and then, taking η\eta small enough, one recovers the same bound as in (2.21).

Case 3: max⁡(1+a,2+α,a+α)<4​α+4/m\max(1+a,2+\alpha,a+\alpha)<4\alpha+4/m. Let ρ:=3​α+2/m\rho:=3\alpha+2/m. Then ρ>1\rho>1 since

ρ=3​α+2/m=4​α+4/m−α−2/m>2+α−α−2/m=2−2/m≥1.\rho=3\alpha+2/m=4\alpha+4/m-\alpha-2/m>2+\alpha-\alpha-2/m=2-2/m\geq 1.

Then in order to bound the right-hand side, we apply Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality for 1≤q=4​(ρ−α)ρ+α1\leq q=\frac{4(\rho-\alpha)}{\rho+\alpha}:

∫Ωu2​ρ−2​α​(t,x)​𝑑x=∥uρ+α2(t,.)∥Lq​(Ω)q≤C∥∇uρ+α2(t,.)∥L2​(Ω)2∥uρ+α2(t,.)∥L2ρ+αq−2+C∥uρ+α2(t,.)∥L2ρ+α​(Ω)q.\begin{split}\int_{\Omega}u^{2\rho-2\alpha}(t,x)\mathrm{d}x&=\|u^{\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2}}(t,.)\|_{L^{q}(\Omega)}^{q}\\ &\leq C\|\nabla u^{\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2}}(t,.)\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}\|u^{\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2}}(t,.)\|_{L^{\frac{2}{\rho+\alpha}}}^{q-2}+C\|u^{\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2}}(t,.)\|_{L^{\frac{2}{\rho+\alpha}}(\Omega)}^{q}.\end{split} (2.22)

for a constant CC. One then has that

∥uρ+α2(t,.)∥L2ρ+α​(Ω)=∫Ωu​dx≤C​ for all ​t∈(0,T)\begin{split}\|u^{\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2}}(t,.)\|_{L^{\frac{2}{\rho+\alpha}}(\Omega)}&=\int_{\Omega}u\ \mathrm{d}x\leq C\ \text{ for all }t\in(0,T)\end{split} (2.23)

from Lemma 7. We integrate the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality in time and we choose η\eta small enough so that we can absorb the term ∬ΩT|∇uρ2+α2|2​(t,x)​𝑑x​𝑑t\iint_{\Omega_{T}}|\nabla u^{\frac{\rho}{2}+\frac{\alpha}{2}}|^{2}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t in the left-hand side. Then the inequality in (2.21) holds.

Combining (2.21) and (2.14) concludes the proof.

∎

We continue by observing that the integrability of ∇v\nabla v allows us to obtain integrability for powers of uu.

Corollary 13.

Let DD satisfy (1.3)–(1.4) and let u,vu,v be solutions of (1.1). If ∇v∈Lp​(ΩT)\nabla v\in L^{p}(\Omega_{T}) with p>2p>2 then ur∈L1​(ΩT)u^{r}\in L^{1}(\Omega_{T}) for all r∈(0,max⁡{p​α​(m+1)(m+2−p)+,p2​α+p−22​a})r\in\left(0,\max\left\{\frac{p\alpha(m+1)}{(m+2-p)_{+}},\frac{p}{2}\alpha+\frac{p-2}{2}a\right\}\right) where mm is the space dimension.

Proof.

First, if r∈(0,1]r\in(0,1], it is a direct consequence of the mass estimate in Lemma 7 and Jensen’s inequality.

Then, for r>1r>1 such that r<p2​α+p−22​ar<\frac{p}{2}\alpha+\frac{p-2}{2}a, we use the energy inequality (2.7) from Lemma 11 with ρ:=r\rho:=r. Since ρ+a>pp−2​(ρ−α)\rho+a>\frac{p}{p-2}(\rho-\alpha), one can absorb the right-hand side by the last term of the left-hand side and conclude that ur∈L1​(ΩT)u^{r}\in L^{1}(\Omega_{T}).

Then, for r>1r>1 such that r<p​α​(m+1)(m+2−p)+r<\frac{p\alpha(m+1)}{(m+2-p)_{+}}, the idea here is to use a Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality combined with the previous lemma to deduce a sequence of LpL^{p} spaces where uu belongs. Let ρ≥α\rho\geq\alpha. We define q=2+4​ρm⁡(ρ+α)q=2+\frac{4\rho}{m(\rho+\alpha)}. By the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality [Nir59], there exists C>0C>0 depending on ρ,m,α\rho,m,\alpha and Ω\Omega such that

∥uρ+α2(t,.)∥Lq​(Ω)≤C∥∇uρ+α2(t,.)∥L2​(Ω)2q∥uρ+α2(t,.)∥L2​ρρ+α4​ρm​q​(ρ+α)+C∥uρ+α2(t,.)∥L2​ρρ+α​(Ω).\|u^{\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2}}(t,.)\|_{L^{q}(\Omega)}\leq C\|\nabla u^{\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2}}(t,.)\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{\frac{2}{q}}\|u^{\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2}}(t,.)\|_{L^{\frac{2\rho}{\rho+\alpha}}}^{\frac{4\rho}{mq(\rho+\alpha)}}+C\|u^{\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2}}(t,.)\|_{L^{\frac{2\rho}{\rho+\alpha}}(\Omega)}. (2.24)

Putting (2.24) to the exponent qq, integrating it in time gives

∥u∥Lρ+α+2​ρm​(ΩT)ρ+α+2​ρm≤C(supt∈(0,T)∥u(t,.)∥Lρ2​ρm+supt∈(0,T)∥u(t,.)∥Lρq​ρ+α2)(∥∇uρ+α2∥L2​(ΩT)2+1).\|u\|_{L^{\rho+\alpha+\frac{2\rho}{m}}(\Omega_{T})}^{\rho+\alpha+\frac{2\rho}{m}}\leq C\left(\sup\limits_{t\in(0,T)}\|u(t,.)\|_{L^{\rho}}^{\frac{2\rho}{m}}+\sup\limits_{t\in(0,T)}\|u(t,.)\|_{L^{\rho}}^{q\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2}}\right)\left(\|\nabla u^{\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2}}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}+1\right). (2.25)

Now using Lemma 11 with s=0s=0 together with the assumption that ∇v∈Lp​(ΩT)\nabla v\in L^{p}(\Omega_{T}), we know that

supt∈(0,T)∥u(t,.)∥Lρ​(Ω)ρ≤C(∥u0∥Lρ​(Ω)ρ+∥u∥Lpp−2​(ρ−α)​(ΩT)ρ−α+1)\sup\limits_{t\in(0,T)}\|u(t,.)\|^{\rho}_{L^{\rho}(\Omega)}\leq C\left(\|u_{0}\|^{\rho}_{L^{\rho}(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^{\frac{p}{p-2}(\rho-\alpha)}(\Omega_{T})}^{\rho-\alpha}+1\right) (2.26)

and

‖∇uρ+α2‖L2​(ΩT)2≤C⁡(‖u0‖Lρ​(Ω)ρ+‖u‖Lpp−2​(ρ−α)​(ΩT)ρ−α+1).\|\nabla u^{\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2}}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}\leq C\left(\|u_{0}\|^{\rho}_{L^{\rho}(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^{\frac{p}{p-2}(\rho-\alpha)}(\Omega_{T})}^{\rho-\alpha}+1\right). (2.27)

Then reinserting (2.26) and (2.27) in (2.25) we get (using the regularity of the initial data)

‖u‖Lρ+α+2​ρm​(ΩT)ρ+α+2​ρm≤C⁡(1+‖u‖Lpp−2​(ρ−α)​(ΩT)(ρ−α)​(1+q​ρ+α2​ρ)).\|u\|_{L^{\rho+\alpha+\frac{2\rho}{m}}(\Omega_{T})}^{\rho+\alpha+\frac{2\rho}{m}}\leq C\left(1+\|u\|_{L^{\frac{p}{p-2}(\rho-\alpha)}(\Omega_{T})}^{(\rho-\alpha)(1+q\frac{\rho+\alpha}{2\rho})}\right). (2.28)

For η0>1\eta_{0}>1, let us define ρ0>α\rho_{0}>\alpha by η0=pp−2​(ρ0−α)\eta_{0}=\frac{p}{p-2}(\rho_{0}-\alpha), and let us define the sequences (ηk)k(\eta_{k})_{k} and (ρk)k(\rho_{k})_{k} recursively as

ηk+1=ρk+α+2​ρkm,ηk+1=pp−2​(ρk+1−α),k≥0.\eta_{k+1}=\rho_{k}+\alpha+\frac{2\rho_{k}}{m},\qquad\eta_{k+1}=\frac{p}{p-2}(\rho_{k+1}-\alpha),\qquad k\geq 0. (2.29)

By definition of these sequences, (2.28) gives that if u∈Lηk​(ΩT)u\in L^{\eta_{k}}(\Omega_{T}) then u∈Lηk+1​(ΩT)u\in L^{\eta_{k+1}}(\Omega_{T}).

We can write, for all k≥0k\geq 0,

so that studying the limit we get that in the limit k⟶∞k\longrightarrow\infty

ηk⟶α​p​(1+m)2+m−p\displaystyle\eta_{k}\longrightarrow\frac{\alpha p(1+m)}{2+m-p}\qquad if ​p<m+2,\displaystyle\text{ if }p<m+2, (2.31)
ηk⟶∞\displaystyle\eta_{k}\longrightarrow\infty\qquad if ​p≥m+2,\displaystyle\text{ if }p\geq m+2, (2.32)

and that concludes the proof. ∎

2.3. Transfer of integrability from uu to ∇xv\nabla_{x}v

We prove that we can transfer the integrability of uu to ∇xv\nabla_{x}v. To get this result we make use of Wp1,2W^{1,2}_{p} estimates that we recall from [LSU68, Theorem 9.1 Chapter 5 and remark p.351] and [VT08, Lemma 2.2].

Lemma 14 (Wp1,2W^{1,2}_{p} estimates).

Let 3<q<∞3<q<\infty, w0∈Wq2​(Ω)w_{0}\in W^{2}_{q}(\Omega) and ww be the unique solution in Wq1,2​(ΩT)W^{1,2}_{q}(\Omega_{T}) of the equation

{wt−a⁡(t,x)​Δ​w=f⁡(t,x)(t,x)∈ΩT,∇w⋅n=0x∈∂Ω,t>0,w⁡(t0,x)=w0x∈Ω\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}w_{t}-a(t,x)\Delta w=f(t,x)&(t,x)\in\Omega_{T},\\ \nabla w\cdot n=0&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ w(t_{0},x)=w_{0}&x\in\Omega\end{array}\right. (2.33)

where a⁡(t,x)a(t,x) is a continuous function on ΩT¯\overline{\Omega_{T}} satisfying

0<λ≤a⁡(t,x)≤Λ,∀(t,x)∈ΩT¯,0<\lambda\leq a(t,x)\leq\Lambda,\quad\forall(t,x)\in\overline{\Omega_{T}},

where λ\lambda and Λ\Lambda are positive constants. We assume that f∈Lq​(ΩT)f\in L^{q}(\Omega_{T}). Then there exists a constant cq>0c_{q}>0 depending on q,T,λq,T,\lambda and Λ\Lambda such that

‖w‖Wq1,2​(ΩT)≤cq​(‖f‖Lq​(ΩT)+‖w0‖Wq2​(ΩT)),\|w\|_{W^{1,2}_{q}(\Omega_{T})}\leq c_{q}\left(\|f\|_{L^{q}(\Omega_{T})}+\|w_{0}\|_{W^{2}_{q}(\Omega_{T})}\right),

where w0w_{0} satisfies ∇w0⋅n=0\nabla w_{0}\cdot n=0 on ∂Ω\partial\Omega.

Corollary 15 (Transfer of integrability from uu to ∇v\nabla v).

Let DD satisfy (1.3)–(1.4) and let u,vu,v be solutions of (1.1) with vv uniformly continuous on ΩT\Omega_{T}. If ud∈Lp​(ΩT)u^{d}\in L^{p}(\Omega_{T}) for p∈[2,+∞)p\in[2,+\infty) then ∇v∈L2​p​(ΩT)\nabla v\in L^{2p}(\Omega_{T}).

Proof of Corollary 15.

Recall the function w=(dv+dγ​⟨v⟩γ)​vw=(d_{v}+d_{\gamma}\langle v\rangle^{\gamma})v and its equation in (2.16). See that vv is uniformly continuous in ΩT\Omega_{T} so continuous in ΩT¯\overline{\Omega_{T}}. Combining the Lemmas 14 and 8, both ∇w\nabla w and ∇v\nabla v are in L2​p​(ΩT)L^{2p}(\Omega_{T}) since

∇w=(du+dγ⟨v⟩γ+γ​dγ​v2⟨v⟩2−γ)∇v.\nabla w=\left(d_{u}+d_{\gamma}\langle v\rangle^{\gamma}+\frac{\gamma d_{\gamma}v^{2}}{\langle v\rangle^{2-\gamma}}\right)\nabla v.

∎

2.4. Iteration and conclusion

We deduce using the previous subsections that uu and ∇v\nabla v are in any LpL^{p} space.

Lemma 16.

Let uu and vv be solutions of (1.1) where DD satisfies (1.4). Then uu and ∇v\nabla v are in Lp​(ΩT)L^{p}(\Omega_{T}) for all p∈(1,∞)p\in(1,\infty) with a bound only depending on pp, the initial data, DD, TT, Ω\Omega and mm.

Proof.

Let us prove that vv is uniformly continuous in Ω\Omega to be able to apply Corollary 15. By Proposition 12 we have that ∇v∈L4​(ΩT)\nabla v\in L^{4}(\Omega_{T}), so we can apply Corollary 13 with p=4p=4 and deduce that u∈Lr​(ΩT)u\in L^{r}(\Omega_{T}) for any r<max⁡(4​α​(m+1)(m−2)+,2​α+a)r<\max\left(\frac{4\alpha(m+1)}{(m-2)_{+}},2\alpha+a\right). Therefore ud∈Lr′​(ΩT)u^{d}\in L^{r^{\prime}}(\Omega_{T}) for any r′<(4​α​(m+1)d​(m−2)+,2​α+ad)r^{\prime}<\left(\frac{4\alpha(m+1)}{d(m-2)_{+}},\frac{2\alpha+a}{d}\right) where thanks to the condition d<max⁡(8​α​(m+1)(m2−4)+,4​α+2​am+2)d<\max\left(\frac{8\alpha(m+1)}{(m^{2}-4)_{+}},\frac{4\alpha+2a}{m+2}\right) in (1.4), we can choose r′>m+22r^{\prime}>\frac{m+2}{2}. We know that vv is solution of the following equation in divergence form

∂tv−∇⋅((dv+dγ(1+γv2⟨v⟩2⟨v⟩γ))∇v)=v(rv−rc⟨v⟩c−rd⟨u⟩d),\partial_{t}v-\nabla\cdot\left(\left(d_{v}+d_{\gamma}(1+\gamma\frac{v^{2}}{\langle v\rangle^{2}}\langle v\rangle^{\gamma})\right)\nabla v\right)=v(r_{v}-r_{c}\langle v\rangle^{c}-r_{d}\langle u\rangle^{d}),

where the diffusion coefficient (dv+dγ​(1+γ​v2⟨v⟩2​⟨v⟩γ))\left(d_{v}+d_{\gamma}(1+\gamma\frac{v^{2}}{\langle v\rangle^{2}}\langle v\rangle^{\gamma})\right) is bounded and the right-hand side v⁡(rv−rc​⟨v⟩c−rd​⟨u⟩d)v(r_{v}-r_{c}\langle v\rangle^{c}-r_{d}\langle u\rangle^{d}) in Lr′​(ΩT)L^{r^{\prime}}(\Omega_{T}) for some r′>m+22r^{\prime}>\frac{m+2}{2}. Applying [DiB93, Theorem 1.3, p. 43] or [LSU68, Theorem 10.1, p. 204], we deduce that vv is Hölder continuous. So in particular uniformly continuous in ΩT\Omega_{T}.

Notice now that Corollaries 13 and 15 give the following sequence of implications

∇v∈Lp​(ΩT)⇒ud∈Lp​(ΩT)⇒∇v∈L2​p​(ΩT)⇒ud∈L2​p​(ΩT).\nabla v\in L^{p}(\Omega_{T})\Rightarrow u^{d}\in L^{p}(\Omega_{T})\Rightarrow\nabla v\in L^{2p}(\Omega_{T})\Rightarrow u^{d}\in L^{2p}(\Omega_{T}). (2.34)

Therefore ∇v∈L4​(ΩT)\nabla v\in L^{4}(\Omega_{T}) yields immediately the result. ∎

Remark 17.

We remark here that one can obtain an Lp​(Ω)L^{p}(\Omega)-estimate for the ∇u\nabla u as in equation (2.10) in Lemma 12 uniformly in time following the proof proposed in [TW19, Prop. 3.4]. If one further assumes convexity of the domain, following [TW19] one can make the estimates in Lemma 16 uniform in time under additional assumptions on the parameters.

3. L∞L^{\infty} estimate for uu and proof of the main Theorem

We now prove our main theorem. We first prove that the solution uu of (1.1) is bounded on ΩT\Omega_{T}, and then conclude thanks to classical Hölder and Schauder estimates.

Lemma 18.

For any solution u:ΩT→ℝu:\Omega_{T}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} of (1.1) with DD satisfying (1.4), the following estimate holds true,

‖u‖L∞​(ΩT)≤C⁡(T),\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C(T),

where C⁡(T)C(T) only depends on the initial data, DD, TT, Ω\Omega and mm.

Proof.

The result can be obtained with the Moser iteration technique, see [TW19], [TW11, Appendix A]. For the paper to be self-contained we present our proof: it relies on the De-Giorgi technique. The details are presented in the Appendix A. We prove separately the boundedness on (0,T2)×Ω\left(0,\frac{T}{2}\right)\times\Omega and (T2,T)×Ω\left(\frac{T}{2},T\right)\times\Omega.

First by a Sobolev embedding (see for example [AF03, Theorem p.85]) since by Theorem 2, u∈C⁡([0,T),W1,p0​(Ω))u\in C(\left[0,T\right),W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega)), we deduce

supt∈[0,T2]‖u(t,.)‖L∞​(Ω)≤Csupt∈[0,T2]||u(t,.)||W1,p0​(Ω)≤C(T).\sup_{t\in\left[0,\frac{T}{2}\right]}\left\|u(t,.)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq C\sup_{t\in\left[0,\frac{T}{2}\right]}||u(t,.)||_{W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega)}\leq C(T).

Then apply Lemma 20 with τ1=0\tau_{1}=0 and τ2=T2\tau_{2}=\frac{T}{2} to δ​u‖u‖Lm+3​(ΩT)+δ\frac{\delta u}{\|u\|_{L^{m+3}(\Omega_{T})}+\delta} which still satisfies the energy estimate (A.1) for ρ=m+3\rho=m+3, to deduce that uu is bounded in (T2,T)×Ω\left(\frac{T}{2},T\right)\times\Omega which ends the proof. ∎

We now conclude the proof of Theorem 1 using the classical Hölder and Schauder estimates.

Proof.

Let us define A⁡(t,x),F⁡(t,x)A(t,x),F(t,x) and f⁡(t,x),B⁡(t,x)f(t,x),B(t,x) and g⁡(t,x)g(t,x) as follows,

A⁡(t,x)=du+dα​(1+α​u2⟨u⟩2)​⟨u⟩α+dβ​⟨v⟩β,A(t,x)=d_{u}+d_{\alpha}(1+\alpha\frac{u^{2}}{\langle u\rangle^{2}})\langle u\rangle^{\alpha}+d_{\beta}\langle v\rangle^{\beta},
F(t,x)=βdβu​v⟨v⟩2−β∇v=G(t,x)∇v,F(t,x)=\beta d_{\beta}\frac{uv}{\langle v\rangle^{2-\beta}}\nabla v=G(t,x)\nabla v,
f⁡(t,x)=u⁡(ru−ra​⟨u⟩a−rb​⟨v⟩b).f(t,x)=u(r_{u}-r_{a}\langle u\rangle^{a}-r_{b}\langle v\rangle^{b}).

Then uu is a solution of

∂tu−∇⋅(A(t,x)∇u)+∇⋅F=f.\partial_{t}u-\nabla\cdot(A(t,x)\nabla u)+\nabla\cdot F=f.

Let us define B⁡(t,x)B(t,x) and g⁡(t,x)g(t,x) as follows,

B⁡(t,x)=dv+dγ​(1+γ​v2⟨v⟩2)​⟨v⟩γ,B(t,x)=d_{v}+d_{\gamma}(1+\gamma\frac{v^{2}}{\langle v\rangle^{2}})\langle v\rangle^{\gamma},
g⁡(t,x)=v⁡(rv−rc​⟨v⟩c−rd​⟨u⟩d).g(t,x)=v(r_{v}-r_{c}\langle v\rangle^{c}-r_{d}\langle u\rangle^{d}).

Then vv is a solution of

∂tv−∇⋅(B(t,x)∇v)=g.\partial_{t}v-\nabla\cdot(B(t,x)\nabla v)=g.

From Lemmas 7, 16 and 20, there are constants Λ>0\Lambda>0 and C>0C>0 such that

Λ−1≤A⁡(t,x)≤ΛandΛ−1≤B⁡(t,x)≤Λ∀(t,x)∈ΩT,\Lambda^{-1}\leq A(t,x)\leq\Lambda\quad\text{and}\quad\Lambda^{-1}\leq B(t,x)\leq\Lambda\quad\forall(t,x)\in\Omega_{T},
‖f‖L∞​(ΩT)+‖g‖L∞​(ΩT)≤C,\|f\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})}+\|g\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C,
‖F‖Lp​(ΩT)≤Cfor any ​p∈(2,∞).\|F\|_{L^{p}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C\quad\mbox{for any }p\in(2,\infty).

Using for both uu and vv the classical Hölder regularity theory [LSU68, Theorem 10.1, p.204] or [DiB93, Theorem 1.3, Remark 1.1 p.43], there exists constants ϖ∈(0,1)\varpi\in(0,1) and C⁡(T)>0C(T)>0 such that

‖u‖Cϖ,ϖ2​(ΩT¯)≤C⁡(T)and‖v‖Cϖ,ϖ2​(ΩT¯)≤C⁡(T).\|u\|_{C^{\varpi,\frac{\varpi}{2}}(\overline{\Omega_{T}})}\leq C(T)\quad\text{and}\quad\|v\|_{C^{\varpi,\frac{\varpi}{2}}(\overline{\Omega_{T}})}\leq C(T).

We define w=(dv+dγ​⟨v⟩γ)​vw=(d_{v}+d_{\gamma}\langle v\rangle^{\gamma})v and w¯=(du+dα​⟨u⟩α+dβ​⟨v⟩β)​u\bar{w}=(d_{u}+d_{\alpha}\langle u\rangle^{\alpha}+d_{\beta}\langle v\rangle^{\beta})u which solves

∂tw=B⁡(t,x)​Δ​w+B⁡(t,x)​g​(t,x),\partial_{t}w=B(t,x)\Delta w+B(t,x)g(t,x),

and

∂tw¯=A⁡(t,x)​Δ​w¯+A⁡(t,x)​f​(t,x)+G⁡(t,x)​Δ​w+G⁡(t,x)​g​(t,x),\partial_{t}\bar{w}=A(t,x)\Delta\bar{w}+A(t,x)f(t,x)+G(t,x)\Delta w+G(t,x)g(t,x),

with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. We apply the Schauder estimate [LSU68, Theorem 5.3, pp.320-321] first to ww since the coefficients in the equation of ww are Hölder continuous, to obtain

‖v‖C2+κ2,2+κ​(ΩT¯)≤C⁡(T),\|v\|_{C^{\frac{2+\kappa}{2},2+\kappa}(\overline{\Omega_{T}})}\leq C(T),

where κ∈(0,ν].\kappa\in\left(0,\nu\right]. Using the last estimate and the Schauder estimate for the equation of w¯\bar{w}, we get

‖u‖C2+μ2,2+μ​(ΩT¯)≤C⁡(T),\|u\|_{C^{\frac{2+\mu}{2},2+\mu}(\overline{\Omega_{T}})}\leq C(T),

where μ∈(0,ν]\mu\in\left(0,\nu\right]. Iterating again, it gives u,v∈C2+ν2,2+ν​(ΩT¯)u,v\in C^{\frac{2+\nu}{2},2+\nu}(\overline{\Omega_{T}}) regarding to the initial data. So ∇u\nabla u and ∇v\nabla v are Hölder continuous on ΩT¯\overline{\Omega_{T}} so necessarily (1.6) is satisfied. Consequently, by Theorem 2 the maximal time of the local solutions is tmax=∞t_{\mathrm{max}}=\infty which ends the proof. ∎

Appendix A Boundedness of uu with De Giorgi

In this appendix we get the first lemma of De Giorgi, which is an Lρ−L∞L^{\rho}-L^{\infty} estimate for uu. To this end, we define a relevant class of energy estimate which we call the De Giorgi class by analogy with quasi-linear elliptic and parabolic studies [DiB95, Lie96].

Proposition 19 (The De Giorgi class).

Considering the system of cross-diffusion equations given by (1.1), when α>0\alpha>0 the following energy estimate holds true for any constant ρ>2\rho>2 and any k∈ℝk\in\mathbb{R},

∫Ω(u−k)+ρ​(t,x)​𝑑x+∬(s,t)×Ω|∇(u−k)+ρ2|2​(τ,x)​𝑑x​𝑑τ\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}(u-k)_{+}^{\rho}(t,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x+\iint_{(s,t)\times\Omega}|\nabla(u-k)_{+}^{\frac{\rho}{2}}|^{2}(\tau,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}\tau (A.1)
≲∫Ω(u−k)+ρ​(s,x)​𝑑x+(∬(s,t)×Ω(u−k)+ρ​(τ,x)​𝑑x​𝑑τ)ρ−2ρ\displaystyle\lesssim\int_{\Omega}(u-k)_{+}^{\rho}(s,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x+\left(\iint_{(s,t)\times\Omega}(u-k)_{+}^{\rho}(\tau,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}\tau\right)^{\frac{\rho-2}{\rho}}
+∬(s,t)×Ω(u−k)+ρ−1(τ,x)dxdτ\displaystyle+\iint_{(s,t)\times\Omega}(u-k)_{+}^{\rho-1}(\tau,x){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}\tau

where the constant only depends on the initial data, DD, TT, Ω\Omega, ρ\rho.

We multiply the equation for uu by (u−k)+ρ−1(u-k)^{\rho-1}_{+} and integrate on (s,t)×Ω(s,t)\times\Omega,

+∬(s,t)×Ω((du+dα(1+αu2⟨u⟩2)⟨u⟩α+dβ⟨v⟩β)|∇(u−k)+ρ2|2)dxdt\displaystyle+\iint_{(s,t)\times\Omega}\Big((d_{u}+d_{\alpha}\left(1+\alpha\frac{u^{2}}{\langle u\rangle^{2}}\right)\langle u\rangle^{\alpha}+d_{\beta}\langle v\rangle^{\beta})|\nabla(u-k)_{+}^{\frac{\rho}{2}}|^{2}\Big){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t
=∬(s,t)×Ω(u−k)+ρ−1​u​(ru−ra​⟨u⟩a−rb​⟨v⟩b)​𝑑x​𝑑t,\displaystyle=\iint_{(s,t)\times\Omega}(u-k)_{+}^{\rho-1}u(r_{u}-r_{a}\langle u\rangle^{a}-r_{b}\langle v\rangle^{b}){\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t,

which using the fact that −⟨x⟩a≤−xa-\langle x\rangle^{a}\leq-x^{a} and x⁡(ru−ra​xa)≤Cx(r_{u}-r_{a}x^{a})\leq C for all x≥0x\geq 0, simplifies into

First Lemma of De Giorgi. We get from the De Giorgi class the first lemma of De Giorgi, which is a Lρ−L∞L^{\rho}-L^{\infty} estimate to conclude that uu is bounded.

Lemma 20 (First Lemma of De Giorgi, Lρ−L∞L^{\rho}-L^{\infty} estimate).

Let 0≤τ1<τ2<T0\leq\tau_{1}<\tau_{2}<T and ρ>m+2\rho>m+2. There exists a positive universal constant δ\delta only depending on the initial data, DD, TT, Ω\Omega, mm, ρ\rho such that for any nonnegative function u:ΩT→ℝu:\Omega_{T}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} satisfying the energy estimate (A.1) the following implication holds true. If

∬(τ1,T)×Ωuρ​𝑑x​𝑑t≤δ,\displaystyle\iint_{(\tau_{1},T)\times\Omega}u^{\rho}{\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t\leq\delta,

then we have

u≤12 in ​(τ2,T)×Ω.u\leq\frac{1}{2}\quad\mbox{ in }(\tau_{2},T)\times\Omega.

Uk=∬Ωtk,T(u−ck)+ρ​𝑑x​𝑑t,U_{k}=\displaystyle\iint_{\Omega_{t_{k},T}}(u-c_{k})_{+}^{\rho}\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}t,

where tk=τ1+(τ2−τ1)​(1−12k)t_{k}=\tau_{1}+(\tau_{2}-\tau_{1})\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k}}\right) and ck=12​(1−2−k)c_{k}=\frac{1}{2}(1-2^{-k}). We notice that tkt_{k} goes from τ1\tau_{1} to τ2\tau_{2} and ckc_{k} from 00 to 12\frac{1}{2}. We would like to prove that UkU_{k} satisfies the following induction formula

Uk≤Ck​Uk−2λ,U_{k}\leq C^{k}U_{k-2}^{\lambda},

where C>0C>0 is a universal constant and λ>1\lambda>1 also. Defining Vk=U2​kV_{k}=U_{2k}, the sequence (Vk)(V_{k}) satisfy

Vk≤Ck​Vk−1λ,V_{k}\leq C^{k}V_{k-1}^{\lambda},

and applying [Gue20, Lemma 3.12], we deduce that Vk=U2​kV_{k}=U_{2k} tends to 00 when V0=U0V_{0}=U_{0} is small enough. Moreover we have U0=∬Ωτ1,Tu+ρ​𝑑x​𝑑tU_{0}=\displaystyle\iint_{\Omega_{\tau_{1},T}}u_{+}^{\rho}{\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t and U∞=∬Ωτ2,T(u−12)+2​𝑑x​𝑑t=0U_{\infty}=\displaystyle\iint_{\Omega_{\tau_{2},T}}\left(u-\frac{1}{2}\right)_{+}^{2}{\,\mathrm{d}}x{\,\mathrm{d}}t=0 and we deduce the result.

Let us prove the induction formula. Let us define the Sobolev exponent

σ={2​mm−2 if ​m>2,5 if ​m=2,+∞ if ​m=1,\sigma=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{2m}{m-2}&\mbox{ if }m>2,\\ 5&\mbox{ if }m=2,\\ +\infty&\mbox{ if }m=1,\end{array}\right.
